H1.text: A magnet holds a chain of paper clips. The first clip is held tight, the next one less, and the last one barely. In a whisper game, the message gets weaker down the line.

H2.text: A pull that fades as it travels. Molecules have a pull like this too.

H3.text: Diya is cooking with vinegar. It has acetic acid, a weak acid.

H4.text: Her book says, swap just one hydrogen for chlorine, and the acid becomes almost eighty times stronger. How can one atom change so much?

H5.text: By the end, you will see the pull that makes this happen, and a second effect that switches on only during a reaction.

P1.text: First, a quick reminder. In a bond, two atoms share a pair of electrons, like two kids holding one rope.

P2.text: If one atom is more electronegative, it pulls the pair closer. It gets a small minus charge, called delta minus.

P3.text: The other atom gets delta plus. Now that atom pulls on its own neighbour a little.

P4.text: This pull passed along a chain of sigma bonds is called the inductive effect.

P5.text: It is permanent. It is always there, even when the molecule is just sitting in a bottle.

S1.text: Let's watch it on our molecule bench. Here is a chain of three carbons with a chlorine atom at the end.

S2.text: Chlorine pulls the shared pair of the carbon chlorine bond towards itself. Chlorine becomes delta minus, carbon one becomes delta plus.

S3.text: Carbon one now pulls a little on the bond to carbon two. Carbon two becomes double delta plus, a smaller charge.

S4.text: Carbon three feels even less. Triple delta plus. The pull fades fast, like the paper clips.

S5.text: After about three bonds, the effect is almost zero.

S6.text: Groups that pull electrons show the minus I effect. Halogens, nitro, cyano, carboxy, ester and aryloxy groups.

S7.text: Groups that push electrons show the plus I effect. Alkyl groups like methyl and ethyl are plus I groups.

D1.text: Now back to Diya's vinegar. Why does chlorine make the acid stronger? Step by step.

D2.text: Step one. An acid is strong if it gives away its H plus easily. What is left behind is a negative ion.

D3.text: Step two. In chloroacetic acid, the chlorine pulls electrons through the chain, away from that negative charge.

D4.text: Step three. The negative charge gets spread out, like a heavy bag shared by friends. A spread out charge is more stable.

D5.text: Step four. A more stable ion forms more easily, so the acid gives H plus more easily. It is a stronger acid.

D6.text: More chlorines pull harder. So trichloroacetic acid is stronger still. And a plus I group like methyl does the opposite. It makes an acid weaker.

L1.text: Now the second effect. Take a molecule with a double bond. A double bond has a sigma pair and a pi pair.

L2.text: When an attacking reagent comes near, the whole pi pair shifts to one atom. This is the electromeric effect.

L3.text: Watch. An H plus comes near ethene. The curved arrow starts at the pi pair and ends on the carbon where H plus joins. This is the plus E effect.

L4.text: Now a cyanide ion comes near a C O double bond. The pi pair moves away from the attacked carbon, onto the oxygen. This is the minus E effect.

L5.text: Take the reagent away, and the pi pair goes back. The electromeric effect is temporary. When it acts against the inductive effect, the electromeric effect wins.

B1.text: Compare them side by side. One is always on. The other switches on only when a reagent arrives.

B2.text: Pause and think. You remove the attacking reagent. Which effect is still there?

B3.text: The inductive effect! It is permanent. The electromeric effect vanishes once the reagent leaves.

T1.text: Remember this. Inductive is a pull that never stops. Electromeric switches on only for a reagent.

W2.text: Arrange by acid strength. Acetic acid, formic acid, and chloroacetic acid.

W3.text: Chloroacetic acid has chlorine, a minus I group. It pulls electrons and spreads the charge. Strongest.

W4.text: Formic acid has just a hydrogen there. No push, no pull.

W5.text: Acetic acid has a methyl group, a plus I group. It pushes electrons onto the negative charge. Weakest.

W6.text: So the order is chloroacetic acid, then formic acid, then acetic acid. Their p K a values are about two point nine, three point eight, and four point eight.

X2.text: Some students think the inductive effect is passed equally along the whole chain, however long it is.

X3.text: Wrong. It fades quickly with distance and is almost nothing after three bonds. So a chlorine close to the acid group makes a stronger acid than a chlorine far away.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Questions on arranging acids by strength, sorting plus I and minus I groups, and comparing inductive and electromeric effects.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which of these is the strongest acid? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B, fluoroacetic acid.

A2.text: All three halogens pull electrons. They show the minus I effect.

A3.text: Fluorine is the most electronegative, so it pulls the hardest. The order of pull is fluorine, then chlorine, then bromine.

A4.text: A bigger pull spreads the negative charge more, so fluoroacetic acid is the strongest. Acetic acid, with plus I methyl, is the weakest.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does the inductive effect fade along a carbon chain?

Y3.text: Two. Why is chloroacetic acid stronger than acetic acid?

Y4.text: Three. What is the difference between the plus E and minus E effects?
